I can confirm that not only the result of the jitted function is in the cpu, but the operations are being encoded in the gpu.

I wished to Call Numba functions with CFFI from jax using custom calls 'a la #1870. This works very well when working only on the cpu, and I hoped that I could move GPU buffers to the GPU so that it would always work.
But since device_put is ignored, that won't work.

`device_put` doesn't work in jit'd functions -- a jit'd function can only be run on a single device, unless using the [host_callback](https://jax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/jax.experimental.host_callback.html) module. You can think of a jit'd function as a single operation from the device-placement view.

I'll update the documentation to mention this. I also think we should make device_put an error inside a jit'd function since it doesn't behave as expected outside the function, but maybe there's a good reason for allowing it that I'm not thinking of.

Just found this after hours of debugging. IMO having a function **silently fail**, but **only under JIT** is a bit masochistic. A standard user will attempt to debug their code by stepping out of the JIT, then the silent error will go back into hiding.

I think it would be very helpful for `device_put` to error under JIT.

@smorad thanks for the comment here.

This behavior in `device_put` is quite old, and pre-dates the current APIs for specifying device/sharding within JIT. I think we could probably re-evaluate that decision now. We'll explore what it looks like to make `device_put` error during abstract evaluation. cc/ @yashk2810

issue.body:
Using device_put is supposed to set the device to be sticky, according to the documentation.
Accordingly, I expect that If I sum 2 cpu arrays (or even a sticky-cpu array + gpu array) the result should live on the cpu.
This is the case for non-jitted functions, but is ignored in the case of jitted functions.

See example: 
```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

_cpu = jax.devices("cpu")[0]
_gpu = jax.devices("gpu")[0]

a = jnp.ones(5)
b = jnp.ones(5)

def print_device(txt, x):
    print(txt, x.device_buffer.device())

def cpu_add(a,b):
    a_cpu = jax.device_put(a, _cpu)
    b_cpu = jax.device_put(b, _cpu)
    return a_cpu+b_cpu

print_device("cpu_add no jit", cpu_add(a,b))
print_device("cpu_add jit", jax.jit(cpu_add)(a,b))
```

output
```python
cpu_add no jit: cpu:0
cpu_add jit: gpu:0
```

issue.body:
This uses a trick to create on the fly a numba function inside of jax jitted functions and call it with almost-0 overhead.

This makes HamiltonianSampler be 5 times faster then the previous implementation that had to exit the jitted function and call back into jax. Now HamiltonianSampler is only 50% slower than MetropolisLocal.
Also, we can use the same trick in over places.

The limitation is that it only works for cpu-arrays, not gpu. But we can put a conversion before calling those functions. Besides, indexing in localoperators makes no sense/would be unbearably slow on gpus so that makes sense.

Also, to make this work i need to add a very ugly yet necessary function to operators returning a closure computing the get_conn_flattened with their internal fields inside the closure. That is because numba does not know how to deal with our operators.

issue.body:
The `symmetrizer` in `DenseSymm` is a very sparse matrix. While `jax` does not yet support sparse operations, we can just do this manually (and more efficiently) in this case.

In fact, `symmetrizer` is a COO matrix with
```python
rows = arange(sites * n_hidden)
cols = ...
data = [1., ..., 1.]
```
so only `cols` need to be stored and the "matrix-vector product" to map reduced to full weights reduces to
```python
full_kernel = (kernel.reshape(-1)[cols]).reshape(self.n_sites, -1)
```
This saves memory for storing `symmetrizer`, which becomes important in larger systems, and is also faster:
At least on the CPU, the comparison looks very much in favor of the indexing version (`n_sites=100`, `features=8`):
```python
In[1]: f1 = jax.jit(lambda w: (w.reshape(-1)[symm_cols]).reshape(n_sites, -1))
In[2]: f2 = jax.jit(lambda w: jnp.matmul(symmetrizer, w.reshape(-1)).reshape(n_sites, -1))
In[3]: f1(kernel); f2(kernel); # pre-jit
In[4]: %timeit f1(kernel).block_until_ready()
101 µs ± 1.78 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10000 loops each)
In[5]: %timeit f2(kernel).block_until_ready()
15.7 ms ± 144 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
```

Still todo:
- [x] The code constructs the full `symmetrizer` and then converts it to a COO matrix. This is of course redundant - that code can be rewritten to just create `cols` directly. I'll do that soon; it just requires some more fiddling with indices.

issue.body:
[The `device_put` command in jax silently fails under `jit`.](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/issues/6040) This PR rips out all mentions of `DevicePutTransform`, which would only use the specified device for non-jitted loaders. Users can compile the dataloader to the CPU or GPU by using `jax.jit(loader.next, backend=...)`.

To use the dataloader and model on different devices, simply use two calls to `jit`
```python
batch, _, _ = jax.jit(dataloader.next, backend='cpu')(state)
batch = jax.device_put(batch, jax.devices(backend='gpu')[0])
results = jax.jit(model, backend='gpu')(batch)
```

For users that absolutely must compile the `DataLoader` and their model into one context on different devices, please use [`jax.pure_callback`](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/_autosummary/jax.pure_callback.html).
